output.headline: England's councils to get direct share of income tax from 2028
output.bodyHtml:
Local areas in England are to get a direct share of income tax revenue from 2028, under a big devolution package John Healey will unveil in next week's budget alongside a new £1.5bn borrowing facility for regional mayors and £150m to help councils build capacity.

Andy Burnham has promised that, as a result, local leaders will no longer have to come "cap in hand to Westminster" ahead of the fresh drive to devolve spending power.

Regional mayors have long complained that they are constrained by their limited borrowing power, in contrast to local authorities in the US and some European countries, which commonly issue their own bonds.

The borrowing plan will form part of the devolution package aimed at boosting regional economic growth. This will also include the allocation of an initial £285m "good growth" funding next year, to be spent on local leaders' priorities, which could include housing, transport links or high street regeneration.

Related: Can curry nights and canny advisers help Healey deliver a budget for everyday people?

Healey will also announce £150m of support to help local authorities scale up and build expertise, amid fears in the Treasury about whether some have the capacity to administer increasingly large budgets.

Hailing the plans, Burnham said they would mean local leaders would no longer need to come to the Treasury for approval for each individual project. "I'm calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country. When I became prime minister, I said that if a decision can be made closer to home, it should be.

"Today we're putting that into practice, shifting power out of Westminster and into the hands of the people who know their communities best."

The £285m in "good growth" funding is intended to tide local authorities over until a new system comes into force in 2028, whereby some income tax revenue will be handed directly to their areas to give them longer-term security, an idea first mooted by Healey's predecessor, Rachel Reeves, earlier this year.

More details of how this will work will be announced at the budget. Local leaders are expected to be allowed to keep some of the additional revenues created by a stronger local economy, giving them an incentive to back pro-growth policies.

Healey said: "Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas."

Tax and spending in the UK is more centralised than in many other leading economies, and Burnham experienced the constraints first-hand as mayor of Greater Manchester.

The package has been drawn up in collaboration with No 10 North, which has been holding a weekly "situation room" meeting with local leaders, to ask them about the barriers to promoting economic growth.

This resulted in an announcement this week that the Treasury has called the "green book", which gives guidance on which projects taxpayers should fund. Under the new rules, projects that can be combined to boost growth, a housing and a transport scheme, for example, can be considered together.

A government white paper on "rewiring the state", due to be published after the budget, will set out more details of how the civil service will be reshaped, as more powers are passed down from Whitehall.

Alongside the devolution plans, Healey's first budget is expected to include support for poorer households hit by rising energy costs, and modest tax rises, including on banks. The chancellor has repeatedly said he wants to offer a "breathing space" to households and businesses that have struggled as the war in the Middle East has driven up bills.

These higher costs have also pushed up the interest rates on government borrowing, making it harder for Healey to balance the books.

He will set out how he plans to fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced in the dying days of Keir Starmer's premiership.

However, Healey is not expected to say when the UK will commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence, an issue that was central to his resignation from Starmer's cabinet. This is likely to be delayed until a spending review due at some point next year.
output.standfirst: Chancellor John Healey will give mayors a £1.5bn borrowing facility and £150m capacity fund, working towards a direct income-tax share for local areas from 2028, Burnham's answer to councils coming 'cap in hand to Westminster'.
output.progress: Healey is also handing councils £150m to help them build the capacity to manage bigger budgets.

output.headline: Aung San Suu Kyi 'sounds strong', says son after rare call
output.bodyHtml:
Myanmar's former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years, though he says she is living in near-complete isolation.

"She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong," Kim Aris said. "I don't think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she's been held in solitary confinement from what I gather."

After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. "I'm still not entirely sure where she is," said Aris. "I think it's a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it."

Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. He welcomed the chance to talk, though he said the invitation was part of a "public relations" campaign by the country's military leaders.

The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.

Activists have long demanded "proof of life" for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain's King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.

Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.

"She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she's unaware of what's happening outside of where she is because she's not allowed any newspapers or radio or television," Aris said. "She's been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free."

Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of "state counsellor" under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.

Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used "disproportionate force", but defended the government against accusations of genocide.

Related: Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it's the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar | Steve Bloomfield

Aris said that his mother was never "silent" on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue "could fill volumes". Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.

He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was "always walking on a tightrope", knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.

"The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread," he said. "The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother's situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job."

The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.

Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had "dwindled incredibly" since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi's release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.

"Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what's happening in Burma shouldn't be down to what was being done to the Rohingya," he said, using the country's former name. "And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: 'Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what's happening in Burma.'"
output.standfirst: Kim Aris tells the Guardian his mother sounded well, but remains isolated, likely in solitary confinement, and that the rare call was a military 'public relations' move.
output.progress: She was visited by the Red Cross in August after years of campaigning, and many governments continue to call for her release.

context.text: Her son called the August Red Cross visit 'the first positive development concerning her in more than five years', though he said it must not be the last.

output.headline: Met considers watchdog referral over its handling of 2019 Markle letter
output.bodyHtml:
The Metropolitan police have confirmed they gave a letter to the Duchess of Sussex in 2019 concerning "alleged offending" involving her father, after accusations arose on Friday about Thomas Markle Sr having child sexual abuse images.

Scotland Yard said it had received a letter in January 2019 making a number of allegations about offending outside Britain, and had passed the information on to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's office, though it did not pass it on to "other law enforcement agencies".

The Met said it was considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.

In a statement, a Metropolitan police spokesperson said: "Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS (Metropolitan Police Service) Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

"The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

"The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach."

The Sun newspaper published claims that Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, claimed he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.

On Friday, Meghan said she had been made aware of these allegations by the Met, and that she was "deeply distressed" by them.

The duchess, who is estranged from her father, said in a statement she had broken off contact to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.

Meghan and Prince Harry recently moved back to the UK from the US.

Meghan's father has denied the allegations and told the Daily Mail the accusations were "sick lies".

In a statement on Friday, issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

"In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

"Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."

She later said she had misremembered the year the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.

A spokesperson for the Duchess of Sussex said: "In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.

"If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.

"I think it is reasonable to recognise that she is doing her best to recall the precise timing of events that were not diarised at the time, and that any discrepancy of a few months is an understandable consequence of that passage of time."

Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered "hundreds, if not thousands" of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.

Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.
output.standfirst: Scotland Yard confirmed it passed the 2019 letter about Thomas Markle Sr to the Sussexes' office, and is now reviewing whether to refer itself to the police watchdog over not sharing it with other forces.
output.progress: The Met is reviewing its handling of the case and considering referring itself to the IOPC.

output.headline: Burnham seeks 'honest discussion' on free movement as migration falls
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham says he wants an "honest discussion" with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.

The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes "all the way" and rejoins the EU.

Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, he said: "I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this."

The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement "had very significant challenges associated with it", but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.

Net migration peaked at a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023, due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson's Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic. It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at 171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016.

"It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn't as difficult [as now]," he told the Sunday Times.

"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.

"The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."

Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November, where he has said he will take the opportunity to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.

He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.

The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union. It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.

The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.

Related: Andy Burnham promises 'serious dialogue' over UK's relationship with EU

In the 12 months to June 2016, the month of the Brexit leave vote, net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000, according to the Office for National Statistics. Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however, before the recent sharp fall.

But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.

Nigel Farage said the prime minister's comments were a "total betrayal" of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham's Makerfield constituency.

The Reform UK leader added: "He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty."

Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: "Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.

"The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it."
output.standfirst: The prime minister is weighing options for a new UK-EU relationship before November's summit, with net migration now near half its 2016 level, as critics accuse him of betraying Brexit voters.
output.progress: Net migration has fallen to 171,000 last year, almost half of 2016 levels, from a 2023 peak of 944,000.

output.headline: Hundreds of thousands join peaceful march across France for school repairs
output.bodyHtml:
Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren's demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces deep social and political upheaval in his final months as president.

In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government's heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.

The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government's policing, saying: "Oppression breeds rebellion" and "The right to protest".

But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city's eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.

Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them.

Related: Major protests in Paris and other French cities in challenge to Macron – in pictures

Police fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. At least two people were seriously injured, one in Clermont-Ferrand and another in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off.

The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France. Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been almost 1,000 arrests.

Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that at various street marches across France there were what he called "high-risk groups" who "broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence".

More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, with public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country.

At Saturday's protests, there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed "illegitimate" and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. "I'm out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it's our legal right to protest in the street and I'm here to defend that."

A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: "We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street."

The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must "give in" and address France's social malaise or face repeated protests. "Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week," Mélenchon said.

The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry.

At Saturday's march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: "Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It's not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet." He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue.

Related: NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France game

Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. "I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people's demands."

Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying "Free Hugs", said: "I'm so angry. I'm here to support schoolchildren's demands for better conditions. I'm so proud of them, and we have to stand together."

She said: "I know I'm not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I've prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn."

In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right anti-immigration National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, a frontrunner in next year's presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. "Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd shouted.
output.standfirst: Almost 1,000 people were arrested as police used teargas, water cannon and batons at the fringes of what was, for most marchers, a lighthearted, family demonstration demanding better schools and policing.
output.progress: Police are investigating after children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry during earlier school protests.

output.headline: Police hunt for prisoner who absconded from medical facility
output.bodyHtml:
A manhunt is under way to locate a prisoner who police say "poses a risk both to himself and the public" after he absconded from a medical facility in London.

Anthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday, the Metropolitan police said.

Det supt Melanie Pressley, who is leading the manhunt, said: "We are conducting various significant inquiries to find Lloyd and return him to custody.

"We are concerned he poses a risk both to himself and the public, and would urge anyone who sees him to call 999 immediately. Do not approach him.

"If you have any information, however small, that could help us locate Lloyd, please get in touch with police as a matter of urgency."

The force warned the public not to approach Lloyd, but instead to contact 999 if he is spotted. Lloyd was seen heading in the direction of Catford, police said in a statement on Saturday.

Lloyd was convicted in 2025 of actual bodily harm, according to the Press Association, relating to an incident in Nottinghamshire involving three emergency services workers.

He received a 12-month custodial sentence and was sent to prison. In September he was transferred to the medical facility in Lewisham.

The 38-year-old is white and about 5ft 8in, of medium build with short dark hair.

He was wearing a grey-blue T-shirt, black tracksuit bottoms and white trainers when last seen at about 4.10pm on Friday, police said.

Officers believe Lloyd could be anywhere in the capital. He also has links to Surrey, Sussex, Thames Valley, Hampshire, Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire and Merseyside.

Anyone with information is asked to call 999, quoting the reference CAD4739/23Oct.
output.standfirst: Met police say Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen on Friday in south London, and 'poses a risk to himself and the public'.
output.progress: Detectives are carrying out significant inquiries and appealing for information to locate Lloyd quickly.

output.headline: Rio's Copacabana fills with a million Lula supporters before Brazil's runoff
output.bodyHtml:
More than one million supporters of Brazil's leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio's most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro.

Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election's runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%.

On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.

Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president, who was first elected in 2002, would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: "Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day."

"The people have woken up," Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have swept Brazil since the leftist's first-round defeat, many led by students.

"Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again, and we don't want dictatorship. We don't want hatred. We don't want guns. We want a country of love," added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula's storied 50-year political career.

"There's never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes," Silva claimed.

Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, was president from 2019 to 2022, as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.

However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil's 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.

Some experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally, which Rio's City Hall said attracted about 1.1 million people, activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: "WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!"

On Saturday afternoon, Lula attended an even larger rally on Paulista Avenue, in the heart of Brazil's biggest city, São Paulo.

"I'm super excited. Lula's going to win," said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday's demo in Rio.

Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. "We've nothing against the right … what we're against is Bolsonarismo," she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro's father botched the response to Covid during his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.

"I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro's neglect," Moraes said.

Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released, and could even return to government, if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro's fellow plotters, who are now in prison or hiding in exile, may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.

Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: "I'm here to prevent democracy becoming extinct, which is what the Bolsonaro family wants".

Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.

Related: Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we're all in peril | George Monbiot

"It's non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground, whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people," she said.

Many marchers were part of the so-called "Lula's Army", a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.

"Being a soldier in Lula's army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn't a normal election," said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group's members.

"They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now," Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.

Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: "Lula, I'm a person with a disability and I'm here to support you."

"My whole life I've believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death," he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.

Large crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil's second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.

Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil's yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags, and many of the United States too.

"The US is a great nation. Who wouldn't want to be aligned with them?" said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.

"I don't want an alliance with Cuba or Venezuela. I want to move forward," Antonio added. When reminded that Venezuela was currently aligned with the US after Donald Trump's January invasion, he said: "True. But for now, a fully right-wing government hasn't been installed yet. It's in transition."

Antonio Carlos Costa Jr, the 59-year-old owner of a shooting club, complained: "Lula did nothing for the country."

Jair Bolsonaro relaxed gun ownership and buying laws, which security experts agree ended up diverting many firearms to criminal gangs, whereas Lula tightened regulations once again. "Jair Bolsonaro simply gave citizens the right to defend themselves, and his son will do the same," said Costa Jr.

Lula supporters scoff at the idea that Bolsonaro, who has a history of well-documented ties with members of Rio's paramilitary "militia" groups, could rid Brazil of criminality.

"If we vote the militias into power, we will be living in a dictatorship," said Erika Cavalcante, 43, an architect who came to the march with a sign reading: "Don't let the mobsters win."
output.standfirst: Nearly 159 million Brazilians are due to vote on Sunday in a tight runoff between the leftwing incumbent and his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, as both camps' supporters took to the streets.
output.progress: Both camps are mobilising huge grassroots networks, including Lula's 10 million-member WhatsApp campaign group, before Sunday's vote.
